Write a note to a friend about a neighbor's advice about your garden. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the note only.
final_message:
Dear Harold,

You asked how the garden is getting on, and I must report that it is getting on under advice, which is a different thing entirely from getting on by itself.

Our neighbor, Mr. Pettibone, came over the fence on Tuesday, with his hands behind him, in the manner of a man who has inspected a great many gardens and approved of very few. He stood a full minute at the edge of the tomato bed without speaking. I have learned that this is the most dangerous kind of silence. Then he said that I had planted them too close, too early, and on the wrong side of the house; and that otherwise they looked well.

I thanked him. One should always thank a neighbor for advice; it costs nothing, and it is the only way to get him back over the fence again. He then told me that the secret of the whole business is to water in the morning, never at night, except in dry weather, when it is best done at night, unless the moon is waning, in which case it makes no difference whatever. I wrote this down on the back of a seed packet, and have since lost the packet, which I think is the only way to follow the rule.

He is, I will say, a man of great experience. He has raised the same six rows of beans for thirty years, and he speaks of them as another man might of his children, with a mixture of pride and anxiety. Last summer they were eaten by something, he does not know what, and he has not forgiven the whole animal kingdom for it. He advised me to set a lantern among my cabbages, to hang pie-tins from the pear tree, and to speak sharply to the rabbits. I have tried the pie-tins. The birds seem to regard them as a kind of dinner bell, and arrive in larger numbers than before.

Polly says I should take his counsel in the spirit in which it is given, which is to say, partly. She holds that a gardener who does everything his neighbor tells him will end with a very fine neighbor's garden, and none of his own. I think there is wisdom in this; and I have therefore moved nothing, and thanked him twice.

The tomatoes, meanwhile, are doing splendidly, I suppose out of spite.

Come and see them before the frost, and bring your own advice. I have a seed packet to lose it on.

Yours ever,
[name]
